fact_text: The price-to-earnings ratio divides a share's price by its earnings per share, showing how much investors pay for each unit of a company's earnings.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Stock Market Financial Ratios Explained!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: In the speaker's example, a business priced at 100 that earns 20 has a P/E of 5, while one priced at 200 with the same earnings has a P/E of 10.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Stock Market Financial Ratios Explained!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: A low share price alone does not show that a stock is cheap, because dividends, bonus shares and stock splits lower the price without changing the value of the business.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Stock Market Financial Ratios Explained!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: P/E comparisons are meaningful only within one sector, since different business models support different typical multiples.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Stock Market Financial Ratios Explained!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: A lower P/E is not automatically better, because a higher P/E can reflect investors expecting faster future profit growth from the company.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Stock Market Financial Ratios Explained!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Earnings per share is profit after tax divided by the number of shares outstanding, and it is the earnings figure used in the P/E ratio.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Stock Market Financial Ratios Explained!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Bonus share issues raise the share count and lower EPS, while buybacks shrink the count and raise EPS, even though the underlying business has not changed.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Stock Market Financial Ratios Explained!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Two-period EPS growth is the change in EPS divided by prior EPS, times 100; in the example, EPS rising from 7 to 10 gives about 42.86 percent growth.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Stock Market Financial Ratios Explained!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Multi-year EPS growth is best expressed as a compound annual growth rate: last EPS divided by first EPS, raised to one over the number of years, minus one.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Stock Market Financial Ratios Explained!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The Buffett indicator divides total stock market value by GDP and assesses whether the whole market, rather than any single stock, is cheap or expensive.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Stock Market Financial Ratios Explained!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: On the Buffett indicator, a reading below about 75 percent suggests undervaluation, 75 to 90 percent suggests fair value, and above 90 to 100 percent suggests overvaluation.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Stock Market Financial Ratios Explained!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Applying the Buffett indicator to the Pakistan market with 2025 data, the analyst concluded the market was undervalued.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Stock Market Financial Ratios Explained!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Gross margin is gross profit divided by revenue, where gross profit is revenue minus the direct cost of goods sold, measuring the share of sales left after product costs.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Stock Market Financial Ratios Explained!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: In the worked example, revenue of 200,000 with cost of goods sold of 120,000 gives gross profit of 80,000 and a 40 percent gross margin.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Stock Market Financial Ratios Explained!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Operating income, or EBIT, deducts operating costs such as salaries, rent and marketing from gross profit but not taxes or debt payments; operating margin divides it by revenue.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Stock Market Financial Ratios Explained!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Net margin is net income divided by total revenue and shows how much of each unit of sales is kept after all expenses; the worked example gives a 20 percent net margin.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Stock Market Financial Ratios Explained!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Revenue is the total money a company takes in, but costs, salaries and taxes sit between revenue and profit, so revenue alone says little about earnings.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Stock Market Financial Ratios Explained!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Return on invested capital is net operating profit after tax divided by invested capital, which includes equity and debt, and shows how well the business uses the capital supplied to it.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Stock Market Financial Ratios Explained!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: ROIC shows past returns on capital, not future returns, so projecting it forward requires a full understanding of the business.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Stock Market Financial Ratios Explained!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The video's debt-to-equity measure divides total liabilities, including short- and long-term debt, by total equity; a value above 1 means the business leans on borrowing to run its operations.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Stock Market Financial Ratios Explained!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: In the worked example, 20 crore of short-term debt and 30 crore of long-term debt against 40 crore of equity gives a debt-to-equity ratio of 1.25.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Stock Market Financial Ratios Explained!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Debt raised to fund expansion can add revenue and profit, so debt is better judged by whether it finances day-to-day operations or growth.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Stock Market Financial Ratios Explained!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Retained earnings are profits kept after costs, taxes and dividends, used to fund expansion, repay debt or repurchase shares; they appear in the equity section of the balance sheet.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Stock Market Financial Ratios Explained!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: A single period of retained earnings says little, so their trend over about five years reveals more about a company's financial position.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Stock Market Financial Ratios Explained!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Current ratio is current assets divided by current liabilities; a value above 1 means the company's short-term assets exceed obligations due within a year.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Stock Market Financial Ratios Explained!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Current ratios are most informative when compared with same-sector peers and tracked across several years rather than read from a single period.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Stock Market Financial Ratios Explained!' (YouTube transcript, undated)
